title: From Kuka to Hawaii: What the Records Can Still Show
subtitle: Sample report — fictional request, real sources
request: My great-grandfather left for Hawaii in the 1890s. The family story and his papers say he came from Kuka village, Ōshima District, Yamaguchi Prefecture (山口県大島郡久賀村). What was Kuka like when he left, why did so many people leave, which records could name him or his house, and what can I see there today?
answerSummary: Kuka was not an isolated hamlet: by 1897 it had its own police station and post-and-telegraph office, hosted Ōshima District's own products fair, and its economy (like the rest of the district) ran on rice, cotton weaving, inshore fishing and silk alongside citrus and farming.

Ōshima District supplied about three in ten of the 944 people on Japan's first government-contract emigrant ship to Hawaii in 1885; by the time the contract scheme ended in 1894 the whole of what is now Suō-Ōshima town had sent 3,913 of the nation's roughly 29,000 contract emigrants, and emigration continued after 1898 outside the contract system.

No single record will name him and his house on its own. A koseki (family-register) request to Suō-Ōshima Town Hall is the fastest, cheapest lead and is open to a great-grandchild without special justification; alongside it, Meiji passport-issuance registers, Foreign Ministry files on individual emigrants, Hawaii-published directories of Japanese residents and Hawaii's own passenger-manifest index can each independently confirm or extend the story.

This session found and read a real 1889 account that names three Kuka villagers who died in Hawaii within a few years of arrival, and real, reference-coded Foreign Ministry files concerning Yamaguchi's Hawaii-resident nationals and a named case tied to Kuka's neighbouring village — concrete proof that this kind of record survives and can be searched.

Kuka itself can be walked today, and the Japan-Hawaii Emigration Museum — itself a returned emigrant's 1928 house — is a short drive away with a database of about 130,000 Hawaii travel records to search by name.

paragraphs.text: By the 1880s and 1890s, Kuka was one of about eleven villages into which the government had divided Ōshima District (大島郡), the group of islands — chief among them Suō-Ōshima itself — off the Yamaguchi coast in the Inland Sea. Far from a marginal hamlet, Kuka was administratively central to the district: when Ōshima organised its second products fair in March 1897, the ten-day event was built and held in Kuka itself, at a site the organisers' own report locates in “Kuka village, the Ura section” (久賀村字浦). The fair's opening and closing ceremonies were held at a shrine hall the report names 玉祖蛭子社 (the exact reading is not certain from the scanned text), and its prize-giving ceremony — attended by the prefectural governor in person — took place at Kuka's own Kakuhōji temple.

That an entire district's fair, its organising office and its printer's shop could all be based in Kuka points to a working village with real infrastructure, not a remote backwater. Among those who attended the fair's opening were the head of the Kuka police station and the head of the Kuka post-and-telegraph office, meaning that by 1897 Kuka's residents could already send mail and telegrams without leaving the village — a small but real detail for anyone imagining how a family later kept in touch with a member overseas. The trade associations whose leaders attended the award ceremony — a three-county cotton-weaving improvement union, an Ōshima rice-improvement union, a fisheries union and a sericulture union — sketch an economy of small-scale weaving, rice farming on what lowland there was, inshore fishing and silk, alongside the citrus for which the island is known today.

What this research could not establish remotely is a population or household count for Kuka itself in this period. The kind of source that would normally supply one — Yamaguchi Prefecture's annual statistical yearbooks, or a county-level administrative report of the 郡治一斑 type — exists but is catalogued at the National Diet Library as paper-only, outside the internet-accessible Digital Collections this session could search. What the sources agree on is the general shape of the island: mountainous, with limited farmland, wrapped around fishing coves, and reachable chiefly by boat until well into the twentieth century.

sections.heading: Why so many left: the government-contract years and after

paragraphs.text: Kuka's men and women who crossed to Hawaii left as part of one of the best-documented migrations in modern Japanese history. Under an 1885 agreement between the Kingdom of Hawaii and the Meiji government, Japan sent chartered ships of “government-contract emigrants” (官約移民) to work Hawaii's sugar plantations between 1885 and 1894. Suō-Ōshima's own museum states that of the 944 men, women and children aboard the very first ship, which reached Honolulu on 10 February 1885, about three in ten came from Ōshima District — a striking share for one rural district of one prefecture. A missionary priest who travelled to Hawaii himself only a few years later, in 1888–89, tallied the same first ship slightly differently: 677 men, 161 women and 111 children, 948 in all — the kind of small discrepancy that is normal between a contemporaneous count and a later official one, and not worth over-reading.

By the time the contract-emigration scheme ended in 1894, the museum's own figures put the total from the whole of what is now Suō-Ōshima town (all of its old villages, Kuka among them) at 3,913 people — about 13.5% of the roughly 29,000 government-contract emigrants sent from all of Japan. An independent 2023 academic study built on the museum's own digitised records separately estimates that around 4,000 people from the wider Yashiro-jima area (Suō-Ōshima) emigrated to Hawaii in the early Meiji period, a figure in the same range and a useful cross-check on the museum's own count. Ōshima's outsized share had, on the evidence gathered here, at least three reinforcing causes: a mountainous island with little level farmland to support a growing population; an existing regional culture of 出稼ぎ — working away from home, whether on Inland Sea shipping or seasonal labour — that made a longer voyage a difference of degree rather than kind; and a real shortage of cash that the emigration companies' advanced fares and Hawaii's contract wages could answer. That the fare itself was a genuine barrier, one that local patrons sometimes bridged, shows in the case of a benefactor in neighbouring Yashiro village who personally arranged financing so that 35 fellow villagers could afford to travel abroad — the same pattern, on a smaller scale, that a family story of borrowed passage money often reflects.

Those who went did not simply vanish from Kuka's account books. The museum describes remittances that supported families at home and funded donations to shrines and schools in the sending villages, and after Hawaii's 1898 annexation by the United States, emigration from the island continued outside the old contract system, with many Ōshima natives becoming established figures in Hawaii's Japanese community. Some contract labourers, of course, never returned at all: the 1889 missionary account is explicit that his tally of 187 dead, recorded by personally visiting graves and reading Buddhist sutras over them, includes people identified as being from Ōshima District, Kuka named among the villages, who died in the islands within a few years of arrival — a sobering context for any family story of a relative who “went to Hawaii” in this period and was, for a time, not heard from.

sections.heading: The records trail: what could name him or his house

paragraphs.text: No single record is likely to answer the whole question by itself; family-history research into this period in Japan usually means combining several imperfect ones. The most direct is the koseki (戸籍), Japan's household-based family register, which — once the household is identified — can show a head of household, spouses, children, and the exact registered domicile (本籍) down to the house-lot, plus any move, marriage, birth or death later recorded in it. For a household in what is now Suō-Ōshima town, requests go by mail to the town hall's Family Register Section: a printed request form, a photocopy of the requester's government ID, a fee paid by postal money order (450 yen for a current family-register transcript, 750 yen for a closed or reorganised one) and a stamped, self-addressed return envelope are all that is required. Crucially, the law allows the person themself, a spouse, or any direct ancestor or descendant — a great-grandchild included — to request it without having to justify why; anyone else must state a specific legal reason.

The main practical risk is not eligibility but time. Closed family registers (除籍簿) must now be kept for 150 years from closure, but that rule only dates to a 2010 reform; before it the period was 80 years, so a register closed long ago may already have been legally destroyed. A related but separate record, the address-history attachment to the koseki (戸籍の附票), has had its own 150-year rule only since a 2019 reform, and a copy whose old five-year period had already lapsed by then — that is, closed on or before 19 June 2014 — can no longer be issued. Neither obstacle can be known in advance; only the request itself will show what still survives.

Behind the koseki sits a thinner layer of paperwork created because the family member left the country. Meiji Japan required a passport for overseas travel, and prefectures compiled 旅券下付表 (passport issuance registers) recording when and where each was issued; surviving volumes are now mostly held by the National Archives of Japan, and this research located two such registers covering January 1888 to March 1891 — the heart of the contract-emigration years — one of them compiled by Kanagawa Prefecture specifically (reference code A03032300800, with a companion volume A03032300700). A Yamaguchi-specific volume for the same years was not located in this session and would need a further, on-site search of the National Archives catalogue. A more promising vein is the Foreign Ministry's own case files on individual Japanese nationals abroad, digitised and freely viewable through JACAR, the Asia Historical Records Center: this research found a real, named 1894–95 file created jointly by Yamaguchi Prefecture and the mayor's office of Age-no-shō (安下庄村), Kuka's neighbouring village in Ōshima District, over one villager's military-conscription status while he was overseas (reference code B07090129800), and a 1922–24 exchange between the Yamaguchi governor and the Japanese consul-general in Honolulu over conscription travel costs for the prefecture's Hawaii residents (B07090141600). No equivalent Kuka file was found by keyword search, but the same series is organised by volume and rewards browsing directly rather than only searching by keyword.

On the Hawaii side, two further kinds of record are worth checking in parallel. Hawaii-published directories of notable or successful Japanese residents — a genre this research read directly, in a 1927 example — recorded a subject's exact birth date, registered domicile down to the village, Hawaii address, occupation and a short career narrative; being included required some local prominence, but even a family copy of such a directory, or a citation to one, is a lead worth following. More systematically, the Hawaii State Archives holds an index to all ship passenger manifests from 1843 to 1900, organised by nationality and then surname, recording name, age, occupation, co-travelling family members, the ship, and the exact arrival or departure date; part of this index is on the Archives' own Digital Archives site, though the Japanese-specific portion may still require a Research Room visit or a written request. The Emigration Museum in Suō-Ōshima keeps a further, purpose-built resource of its own: a database room where visitors can search roughly 130,000 Hawaii travel records, official contract emigrants and independent travellers together — the single most efficient place to test whether a specific name and village turn up at all.

sections.heading: What this session checked, and what it could not

paragraphs.text: This sample was researched entirely at a distance, in one working session, using only sources open to remote reading or query. We searched the National Diet Library's Digital Collections two ways: its cataloguing search, which found 1,399 distinct bibliographic records mentioning Suō-Ōshima or Ōshima District in some field, and its full-text search of digitised page images, which can find the exact scanned page (“frame”) of a book where two phrases — say, 久賀村 and 布哇 (Hawaii) — appear together, even inside books the Library restricts to its own premises or to registered users. Of the internet-open books that search surfaced, we opened and read two in full through the Library's OCR text service: an 1889 missionary's travel account that turned out to record, by name, three Kuka residents who died in Hawaii in 1888–89, and an 1897 report of a district products fair that turned out to have been held in Kuka village itself. Both are cited above with their exact page numbers so the client, or anyone else, can open the same pages online.

We separately queried the Asia Historical Records Center's (JACAR) own search system directly — it is not part of the Digital Collections — and found real, reference-coded Foreign Ministry files, described above, concerning Yamaguchi Prefecture's Hawaii-resident nationals and a named villager from Kuka's neighbouring village. We also read the current, official web pages of Suō-Ōshima Town (for the museum, and for the exact koseki mail-request procedure), the Japan-Hawaii Emigration Museum's own site, the Yamaguchi Prefectural Archives, the Hawaii State Archives, and two Japanese municipalities' official explanations of the family-register retention rules, all checked on 28 September 2026.

Three things this session could not verify remotely, and a genuine Deep Research engagement would need to chase on-site. First, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' own Diplomatic Archives website was unreachable from this session — a network restriction here, not a content problem — so its current reading-room procedures rely here on the National Diet Library's own guide to pre-war travel records rather than the Archives' page directly. Second, the Geospatial Information Authority's map- and aerial-photograph-ordering service was likewise unreachable; we confirmed programmatically, from the Authority's public photograph archive, that the oldest aerial photograph covering Kuka in that archive dates only to 1961–69, but we could not identify which old paper topographic-map sheet, if any, shows Kuka from the Meiji or Taishō era. Third, and most important for a real client, no Kuka-specific population or household figure, and no Kuka-specific passport register or conscription file, turned up in this session; all three look likely to exist only on paper, in a local or prefectural archive, or in a JACAR series that needs volume-by-volume browsing rather than a keyword search — exactly the kind of gap an on-site visit, or a longer engagement, is for.

A realistic next stage moves outward from the family record to the country: first the koseki, because it is cheap, fast and needs no travel; then Suō-Ōshima itself, where the museum's own database and the physical village can be checked in the same trip; then the national archives, which between them hold the passport and consular paperwork; and only then, if a specific ship, year or name emerges, the Hawaii-side manifests and any temple or cemetery records on that end.

In practice we would request the koseki by mail before travelling at all, since the reply — or its absence — tells the researcher what to look for on the ground. We would visit the Emigration Museum and walk Kuka itself, including the harbour area (字浦) named in the 1897 fair report, asking locally after the shrine and temple it mentions, since well over a century of consolidation may have changed a building's name even where the site survives. Only if a name, date or reference code from the museum or the koseki points somewhere specific would we follow it into the Yamaguchi Prefectural Archives' catalogue, and from there into the National Archives and Diplomatic Archives material in Tokyo, most of which can be requested as copies without a researcher needing to be present for everything. The Hawaii-side check — the passenger-manifest index and, if a temple affiliation is known, that temple's own registers — can run in parallel by post or email throughout.

Kuka is a real, inhabited part of Suō-Ōshima town today, on the island's north side around its own small harbour. Nothing this research reviewed suggests the kind of dramatic change that erases a place: no wartime destruction, and no large reclamation project, is recorded for this stretch of coast in the sources checked here. Comparing the earliest aerial photograph of the hamlet held in the national online archive, from 1961–69, with the most recent orthophoto shows a settlement that has grown modestly rather than been rebuilt from nothing — worth confirming on foot, since the online archive itself has no earlier images to compare against.

The single most tangible link between Kuka's story and the present is a short drive away, at the Japan-Hawaii Emigration Museum on the island's western side. The museum is not a purpose-built structure but the actual house of Fukumoto Chōemon, a Suō-Ōshima man who returned from Hawaii in 1924 and built it in 1928 at a cost the museum itself puts at about 30,000 yen then — by its own estimate, upward of 300 million yen today. The house's blend of Japanese and Western styles is itself a physical record of what a successful return from Hawaii could look like, and it was formally recognised as a national Registered Tangible Cultural Property in February 2022. Inside, the museum's database room is where a family name first meets the record, and its displays of tools and photographs brought back by returnees are the closest most visitors will get to seeing what emigrant life actually involved.

None of this amounts to standing in front of a house we can say was his. What it does offer is a village that can be walked, a record system with a clear — if not guaranteed — path into it, and a museum built for exactly this kind of question. Whether his name surfaces in a koseki reply, a conscription file, a ship's manifest or a temple register is the work the next tier of this report, or a visit, is for.

recordsTrail.record: Koseki and closed-register (除籍/改製原戸籍) extracts for the household
recordsTrail.holder: Suō-Ōshima Town Hall, Family Register Section (戸籍住基班) — the present-day registry office for the former Kuka village
recordsTrail.whatItCanShow: Head of household, family members, and births, marriages and deaths later recorded in it; the koseki-no-fuhyō variant shows the registered-domicile address history
recordsTrail.access: By mail, from the person, a spouse, or a direct ancestor/descendant (a great-grandchild qualifies) with an ID copy and fee; anyone else must state a specific legal reason

recordsTrail.record: Meiji-era passport issuance registers (旅券下付表)
recordsTrail.holder: Originally the issuing prefecture; surviving volumes mostly at the National Archives of Japan, some digitised via JACAR
recordsTrail.whatItCanShow: Date and place of passport issue; where a full volume survives, the traveller's name and destination
recordsTrail.access: Digitised volumes viewable free via JACAR; non-digitised volumes require an in-person or written National Archives request

recordsTrail.record: Foreign Ministry files on individual emigrants abroad (e.g. 本邦人徴兵関係雑纂, conscription-abroad miscellany)
recordsTrail.holder: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (外交史料館), digitised via JACAR
recordsTrail.whatItCanShow: A named emigrant's home village and situation abroad, via correspondence between the prefecture, his village mayor's office and the consulate
recordsTrail.access: Free to view online via JACAR for digitised items; the series can be browsed volume by volume as well as searched

recordsTrail.record: Hawaii-published directories of Japanese residents (banzuke/meikan, e.g. 布哇日本人銘鑑)
recordsTrail.holder: Published in Hawaii; copies at the National Diet Library (some open online) and at Hawaii/US libraries
recordsTrail.whatItCanShow: Name, exact birth date, registered domicile down to the village, Hawaii address, occupation and a short career account, for those included
recordsTrail.access: Several editions readable online at the National Diet Library now; others require in-person or registered-user access

recordsTrail.record: Hawaii ship passenger manifests and their 1843–1900 index
recordsTrail.whatItCanShow: Name, age, occupation, co-travelling family, ship, and arrival or departure date and port
recordsTrail.access: Part of the 1843–1900 index is on the Archives' Digital Archives online; the Japanese-specific portion may need a Research Room visit or written request

recordsTrail.record: The Emigration Museum's own travel-record database (about 130,000 entries)
recordsTrail.whatItCanShow: Whether a name appears among the official and private emigrants indexed from the island, and what detail the entry carries
recordsTrail.access: Search corner on site during opening hours (9:30–16:30, closed Mondays and 29 Dec–3 Jan); no evidence of remote/online public search was found

recordsTrail.record: Meiji/Taishō population, household and industry statistics for Kuka specifically
recordsTrail.holder: Likely Yamaguchi Prefecture's annual statistical yearbooks, or district administrative reports; catalogued paper-only at the National Diet Library
recordsTrail.whatItCanShow: Village-level population and household counts, and industry detail, for Kuka in specific years
recordsTrail.access: Not available online; needs an on-site or by-request paper-catalogue search, e.g. at the Yamaguchi Prefectural Archives

onSitePlan.step: Request the household's koseki and koseki-no-fuhyō by mail, giving the great-grandfather's name, approximate birth year and “Ōshima-gun, Kuka-mura” as the registered domicile
onSitePlan.where: Suō-Ōshima Town Hall, Family Register Section, 126-2 Ōaza Komatsu, Suō-Ōshima-chō
onSitePlan.time: 2–4 weeks by mail from outside Japan

onSitePlan.step: Search the Emigration Museum's database room for the family name and Kuka, and view the exhibits on emigrant life and the government-contract years
onSitePlan.where: Japan-Hawaii Emigration Museum, 2144 Kamikatayama, Nishiyashiro, Suō-Ōshima

onSitePlan.step: Walk Kuka itself, including the Ura harbour area, and ask locally after the shrine and temple named in the 1897 fair report
Search the prefectural document catalogue for Ōshima District/Kuka administrative and statistical papers
onSitePlan.time: 1 day on site, or a written enquiry beforehand

onSitePlan.step: Request or view the National Archives and Diplomatic Archives originals behind any promising JACAR reference codes
onSitePlan.where: National Archives of Japan / Diplomatic Archives reading room, Tokyo

onSitePlan.step: Contact the Hawaii State Archives (and, for post-1900 arrivals, the US National Archives) to search passenger-manifest indexes and request copies
onSitePlan.where: Hawaii State Archives, Honolulu, or by phone/email

tiers.includes: A report to this format for the client's own village or address: full remote search of the National Diet Library's Digital Collections (catalogue and full text), JACAR, and prefectural, municipal, museum and archive websites in Japan and Hawaii; the household's own koseki mail-request form filled in, translated and explained, ready to sign, copy an ID and post; a records trail and on-site plan tailored to the actual family name and village.

Everything in the US$190 tier, plus: submitting the koseki/joseki mail request on the client's behalf as an authorised proxy — with a signed authorisation from an eligible relative, and through a licensed administrative scrivener (行政書士) partner where the relationship needs to be documented — and forwarding what comes back; a half-day search of the relevant museum's or archive's own on-site catalogue or database by a local researcher; and a two-page plain-English digest of anything found.

furtherReading.why: The dedicated local history of Hawaii emigration from Ōshima District; full-text search hits on Kuka/Hawaii terms at frames including 18, 21, 22, 26, 27, 51, 92 and 105. The single most relevant book found this session that could not be read remotely.

furtherReading.why: A Chōshū/Yamaguchi-focused edition of the Hawaii-Japanese biographical-directory genre, with many full-text hits on Ōshima and Yashiro villages (frames including 30, 31, 52, 76, 153, 166, 174, 212, 225, 228). Its editor, Ōkubo Gen'ichi, also appears in a Diplomatic Archives file on Hawaii's Japanese-language press (JACAR B02031115900).

furtherReading.title: 新布哇 (藤井秀五郎著, 1900 and 1902 editions)
furtherReading.why: An early guide to Hawaii with numerous full-text hits on Ōshima villages including Kuka; the 1900 edition's hits include frames 437–457, the 1902 edition's include 441–523. A related, later edition is at pid 767371 and pid 11934916.

furtherReading.title: 大日本海外移住民史 第1編 (1938)
furtherReading.why: A 1938 history of Japanese overseas emigration; catalogued as open online, and NDL full-text search shows Ōshima/Yashiro-village hits at frames 71–74, 215–216, 250, 252, 280 and 288, but this session's attempts to retrieve its OCR text failed (server errors) so it could not be read and cited directly. Worth opening directly in a browser.

furtherReading.title: 日本移民の地理学的研究：沖縄・広島・山口 (石川友紀著, 1997)
furtherReading.why: An academic geography of emigration from Okinawa, Hiroshima and Yamaguchi, with hits on Ōshima/Kuka terms at frames 161, 162, 164, 165 and 168, but restricted to National Diet Library premises.

furtherReading.title: 周防大島民俗誌 (宮本常一著作集, 1997)
furtherReading.why: By Suō-Ōshima's own noted folklorist Miyamoto Tsuneichi; restricted to National Diet Library premises, but likely the richest ethnographic source on the island's pre-war village life, including migration.

deepResearchLeads.what: A Yamaguchi-Prefecture-specific volume of the passport issuance register (旅券下付表) for 1885–1900, and any surviving Ōshima District office original
deepResearchLeads.where: National Archives of Japan catalogue; Yamaguchi Prefectural Archives
deepResearchLeads.how: Search the National Archives' own digital catalogue by creator “山口県” within the 返還文書 series and request a copy; ask the Yamaguchi Prefectural Archives directly whether a prefectural-office original survives.

deepResearchLeads.what: An individual conscription or travel case file for a man from Kuka itself, parallel to the confirmed 1894–95 Age-no-shō file (JACAR B07090129800)
deepResearchLeads.where: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, series 本邦人徴兵関係雑纂, via JACAR or its reading room
deepResearchLeads.how: Browse the series volume by volume by holding institution and date rather than only by keyword, watching for Kuka's mayor's office or Kuka residents by name.

deepResearchLeads.what: A Meiji/Taishō population and household count for Kuka village specifically
deepResearchLeads.where: Yamaguchi Prefecture's statistical yearbooks (山口県統計書) and county administrative reports
deepResearchLeads.how: These are catalogued at the National Diet Library as paper-only; request an on-site reading or scan there, or check the Yamaguchi Prefectural Archives' own document-search system directly.

deepResearchLeads.what: Whether the family's registered domicile is still held in Suō-Ōshima Town's current koseki index
deepResearchLeads.where: Suō-Ōshima Town Hall, Family Register Section
deepResearchLeads.how: Submit the mail-request form with the great-grandfather's name, approximate birth year and “Ōshima-gun, Kuka-mura” as the registered domicile; if the town cannot locate it from that alone, a licensed administrative scrivener (行政書士) in Yamaguchi can search adjoining records on-site.

deepResearchLeads.what: Passenger-manifest confirmation on the Hawaii side, and any temple (Honpa Hongwanji) or cemetery records for a Kuka-born emigrant
deepResearchLeads.where: Hawaii State Archives (1843–1900 manifests); Honpa Hongwanji Mission of Hawaii archives
deepResearchLeads.how: Contact the Hawaii State Archives' Research Room directly by phone or email; for temple records, contact the Honpa Hongwanji Mission of Hawaii's own archives for guidance on the kind of graveyard and membership registers the 1889 account (S1) shows already existed.

deepResearchLeads.what: The specific old topographic map sheet(s) covering Kuka, and any pre-1961 aerial photographs not in GSI's own online archive
deepResearchLeads.where: GSI's map- and aerial-photograph-ordering service (地図・空中写真閲覧サービス); US National Archives cartographic holdings for 1945–50 occupation-era imagery
deepResearchLeads.how: This session could not reach the GSI ordering service (blocked); query it directly by place name or coordinates, or telephone GSI's map-sales counter; for wartime/occupation aerial imagery, search NARA's cartographic record groups.

limits: This is a fictional client and request. No living person's name, address or contact details appear anywhere in this report. The historical individuals named in the 1889 and 1897 sources quoted here are long deceased, drawn from publicly available, out-of-copyright books, and are illustrations of what such records can show — not the fictional client's actual ancestors.

No Meiji-era population or household count specific to Kuka itself (as opposed to Ōshima District or Suō-Ōshima as a whole) was found among the sources open to remote reading; the likeliest sources are paper-only at the National Diet Library and would need an on-site or by-request search.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs' Diplomatic Archives website and the GSI's old-map ordering service could not be reached from this research session (both blocked by network policy); the description of what they hold relies on the National Diet Library's own research guide and on JACAR's digitised holdings, and should be confirmed directly before any client visit.

No historical page images, passenger-manifest scans or koseki forms were downloaded or reproduced in preparing this report; only bibliographic data, archive reference codes, page/frame numbers and our own notes are recorded here, as our sourcing policy requires.
